# NKI heuristics — full rule appendix (generated by merge_heuristics.py)

724 rules from 5 extraction passes. Each rule cites its source; `stated` means the source says it explicitly, `inferred` means derived.


## Where custom kernels pay off (op selection) (56)

- **nl-matmul-wrapper-inserts-transpose** — Prefer nisa.nc_matmul with pre-transposed operands over nl.matmul(x, y) with transpose_x=False.
  - why: nl.matmul is an experimental wrapper; with transpose_x=False it inserts an extra transpose to put x's contraction dim on partitions, costing a PE/Vector pass.
  - when: Hot loops using nl.matmul without transpose_x=True.
  - fix: Load x already transposed (K on partitions) and call nl.matmul(xT, y, transpose_x=True) or nisa.nc_matmul directly.
  - numbers: x_free_max = 128; y_free_max = 512
  - check (static): nl.matmul call with transpose_x omitted or False
  - source: nki.language.matmul docstring  [stated, all]
- **mm-partition-reduce-via-ones** — To reduce along the partition axis, either transpose then tensor_reduce, or multiply by a ones[128,1] stationary tile with nc_matmul.
  - why: Vector Engine reductions only operate on free axes; the Tensor Engine naturally sums across partitions (contraction).
  - when: Attempting nisa.tensor_reduce(axis=0) or looping over partitions.
  - fix: nc_matmul(dst=psum[1,N], stationary=ones[K,1], moving=data[K,N]) gives column sums; or tensor_partition_reduce on GpSimd.
  - check (static): tensor_reduce with axis containing 0
  - source: nki.isa.tensor_reduce docstring, section Layout  [stated, all]
- **transpose-identity-reuse** — Build transpose identities with nl.shared_identity_matrix(n, dtype) rather than ad-hoc constants.
  - why: The compiler dedupes identity matrices of the same dtype across the graph, saving SBUF and loads.
  - when: Multiple nl.shared_constant(np.eye(...)) or iota-built identities.
  - fix: ident = nl.shared_identity_matrix(128, dtype=data.dtype); use as moving in nc_matmul(is_transpose=True).
  - check (static): nl.shared_constant with an identity ndarray argument
  - source: nki.language.shared_identity_matrix docstring  [stated, all]
- **dma-copy-sbuf-to-sbuf-prefer-compute-engine** — For SBUF-to-SBUF movement prefer nisa.tensor_copy (or nc_n_gather/local_gather for gathers) over dma_copy.
  - why: DMA engines have higher latency and are shared bandwidth; on-chip engines move data within SBUF without descriptors.
  - when: dma_copy where both src and dst are SBUF tiles.
  - fix: Replace with nisa.tensor_copy(dst, src) (engine chosen by compiler) or a gather instruction.
  - check (static): dma_copy with buffer(src)==sbuf and buffer(dst)==sbuf
  - source: nki.isa.dma_copy docstring, section Memory types; nki.isa.nc_n_gather docstring  [stated, all]
- **tt-no-free-dim-broadcast-use-tensor-scalar** — For per-partition scalar/vector broadcasts use tensor_scalar (or scalar_tensor_tensor), not a broadcast view into tensor_tensor.
  - why: tensor_tensor requires identical element counts per partition and is slower; tensor_scalar broadcasts a (P,1) operand along the free dim at no extra cost and can fuse two ops.
  - when: nisa.tensor_tensor(data1=x, data2=rowmax.broadcast(1,N), op=nl.subtract).
  - fix: nisa.tensor_scalar(dst, x, nl.subtract, rowmax[(P,1)]) or scalar_tensor_tensor for (x*s)+y.
  - check (static): tensor_tensor where one operand is a broadcast view
  - source: nki.isa.tensor_tensor docstring (note on broadcasting); nki.isa.tensor_scalar docstring  [stated, all]
- **ts-two-ops-same-cost** — Fuse two broadcast ops into one tensor_scalar call ((data op0 operand0) op1 operand1); one op costs the same as two.
  - why: The Vector/Scalar/GpSimd ALU pipeline has two stages per element regardless of use.
  - when: Back-to-back tensor_scalar(multiply) then tensor_scalar(add) on the same tile.
  - fix: nisa.tensor_scalar(dst, x, nl.multiply, s, op1=nl.add, operand1=b).
  - check (static): two consecutive tensor_scalar on same tile each with op1=None
  - source: nki.isa.tensor_scalar docstring  [stated, all]
- **tensor-reduce-negate-free-and-bitvec-int** — Use tensor_reduce(negate=True) to get -sum for free instead of a separate negate; bitvec reductions require integer dtypes and skip casting.
  - why: The negate multiplies by -1 in the output stage at no cost; bitvec ops treat elements as raw bits.
  - when: A tensor_scalar(multiply,-1) after a reduce; bitwise_or reduce on fp tiles.
  - fix: Pass negate=True (arithmetic ops only); cast to int for bitvec reductions.
  - check (static): tensor_reduce(bitvec op) -> int dtypes
  - source: nki.isa.tensor_reduce docstring  [stated, all]
- **exponential-trn3-fast-path** — On trn3 use nisa.exponential(dst, src, max_value=rowmax, reduce_res=rowsum, reduce_cmd=reset_reduce) on Vector Engine for softmax instead of activation(op=nl.exp).
  - why: The dedicated v4 Vector instruction fuses max subtraction and running sum and is faster than the Scalar activation path, also balancing engine load.
  - when: Softmax on trn3 still using Scalar exp for exp+sum.
  - fix: Guard with get_nc_version()==gen4; keep activation path for trn1/trn2.
  - check (static): exponential: nc_version>=4; reduce_init==0 unless reduce_cmd==load_reduce
  - source: nki.isa.exponential docstring; migration/index.rst 0.3.0 'New nki.isa APIs'  [stated, trn3]
- **reciprocal-engine-tradeoff** — Use Vector nisa.reciprocal for small tiles (<64 elements/partition) or when precision matters; use Scalar activation(op=nl.reciprocal) for large tiles (about 8x throughput).
  - why: Vector costs max(MIN_II, 8N) cycles vs Scalar max(MIN_II, N) with MIN_II ~64 cycles; Vector is more precise.
  - when: Hot full-width reciprocal on Vector Engine; precision issues from Scalar reciprocal.
  - fix: Switch engine per tile size; combine with activation scale/bias fusion.
  - numbers: MIN_II = ~64 engine cycles; vector_cycles = 8*N; scalar_cycles = N
  - source: nki/api/nki.api.shared.rst Engine Selection  [stated, all]
- **rsqrt-engine-tradeoff-and-psum** — Choose rsqrt engine deliberately: GpSimd (tensor_scalar(op0=nl.rsqrt, operand0=0.0, engine=gpsimd) / nl.rsqrt) is more precise but 4x slower than Scalar activation(op=nl.rsqrt); nl.rsqrt no longer accepts PSUM inputs.
  - why: Since 0.5.0 nl.rsqrt runs on GpSimd which has no PSUM access.
  - when: nl.rsqrt(psum_tile) compile failure; layernorm rsqrt on GpSimd becoming the bottleneck.
  - fix: Evacuate to SBUF first or call nisa.activation(op=nl.rsqrt) directly.
  - numbers: gpsimd_vs_scalar = 4x slower
  - check (static): nl.rsqrt arg buffer != psum
  - source: nki/api/nki.api.shared.rst Engine Selection; migration/index.rst 0.4->0.5 rsqrt  [stated, all]
- **coll-prefer-implicit-ring** — For ring communication use collective_permute_implicit (+ collective_permute_implicit_current_processing_rank_id) instead of explicit collective_permute pairs.
  - why: Hardware optimizes the implicit ring pattern and the rank id register lets compute overlap communication via dynamic .ap() offsets.
  - when: Explicit source_target_pairs building a ring.
  - fix: Loop over iterations: rank = ..._current_processing_rank_id(it, rg); use register ALU to compute chunk offset.
  - check (static): collective_permute with pairs forming (i, i+1 mod n)
  - source: nki.collectives.collective_permute docstring  [stated, all]
- **nl-divide-prefer-reciprocal-multiply** — Avoid nl.divide in hot paths; compute a reciprocal (Vector nisa.reciprocal or Scalar activation) once per row and multiply with tensor_scalar.
  - why: The api index lists divide as not supported as an ISA op; division lowers to reciprocal + multiply anyway, and the per-partition reciprocal is tiny.
  - when: nl.divide(scores, rowsum_broadcast).
  - fix: nisa.reciprocal(inv, rowsum); nisa.tensor_scalar(out, scores, nl.multiply, inv).
  - check (static): nl.divide call with a (P,1) divisor
  - source: nki/api/nki.language.rst ('.. divide : not supported'); nki.isa.reciprocal docstring  [inferred, all]
- **mm-mx-interleave-cost-planning** — Pay the MX interleave (elements 128 apart packed into quads) offline for weights and fold it into an existing strided VectorE/ScalarE pass for activations; DMA strided interleave is much slower.
  - why: Quantize-MX preserves layout, so the interleaved layout must exist before quantization; on-device TensorCopy with strided access is the fast path, DMA strided access only makes sense when fully hidden behind compute.
  - when: Preparing MXFP8 inputs on trn3.
  - fix: Reshape BF16 [512,512] as [4,128,512] and copy with a strided access pattern into [128, 512, 4], then quantize_mx.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/mxfp-matmul.rst :: SBUF Layout Using Strided Access; Additional Tips  [stated, trn3]
- **op-when-to-write-nki** — Write a custom NKI kernel only for (a) hot regions where the Neuron Compiler's general-purpose lowering under-utilizes hardware, or (b) operators the compiler does not support; otherwise use compiler output or NKI-Lib kernels.
  - why: The compiler already inserts optimized NKI kernels for common ops (vLLM/NxDI models use them); NKI-Lib ships attention, MLP, RMSNorm+quant and collective kernels that beat compiler-generated code.
  - when: Profiler shows engines idle waiting on DMA or gaps in a frequently executed section.
  - fix: Pick a 'minimum cut' subgraph with few inputs/outputs; validate against a numpy reference with representative sizes before optimizing.
  - source: nki/nki_faq.rst :: When should I use NKI?; nki/guides/tutorials/kernel-optimization.rst :: When to write a kernel?; nki/get-started/about/index.rst :: Working with NKI Kernels  [stated, all]
- **op-tensore-native-ops** — Expect dense GEMM, CONV and PF-transpose to be handled well by the compiler on TensorE; spend custom-kernel effort on fusion, layout and data movement around them rather than re-implementing the matmul itself.
  - why: TensorE is 'highly optimized for GEMM, CONV, and Transpose' and holds >90% of core FLOPS; the tutorial matmul reaches 99.5% TensorE utilization only through blocking/DMA work, not instruction tricks.
  - when: Planning a kernel that is mostly a dense matmul.
  - fix: Focus on hoisting loads, blocking all three dims, PSUM bank rotation and output coalescing.
  - source: about-neuron/arch/neuron-hardware/neuron-core-v3.rst :: Tensor Engine; nki/deep-dives/nki_perf_guide.rst :: Opt #8; nki/guides/tutorials/kernel-optimization.rst  [stated, all]
- **op-gather-scatter-is-the-weak-spot** — Treat gather/scatter/indirect patterns (embedding lookups, paged KV cache, interpolation, grid-sample) as the hardest class to make fast: they require software DGE on GpSimd, hwdge cannot gather, and before trn3 no compute engine can gather along the free dim in SBUF.
  - why: Indirect DMA is swdge-only (GpSimd generates descriptors into SBUF); per-row gathers produce small payloads that are descriptor-rate and overhead bound; non-uniform in-SBUF access needs one instruction per vector until NeuronCore-v4 indirect access (no API yet).
  - when: Kernels dominated by vector_offset DMAs or many tiny per-index copies.
  - fix: Restructure data so indices select large contiguous blocks (>= 2 KiB per partition), gather 128 rows per DMA, hoist index generation, and keep GpSimd otherwise idle; consider precomputing gathered layouts on the host.
  - check (static): count dma ops with vector_offset and their bytes per descriptor.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: swdge / hwdge; nki/guides/architecture/trainium3_arch.rst :: SBUF/PSUM indirect access; nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: DGE note  [inferred, all]
- **op-matrix-vector-decode-mapping** — For auto-regressive decode GEMV, keep the large weight tile as stationary ([K=128, M=128] per instruction) and the token vector(s) as moving, and batch tokens/heads into the moving free dim where possible.
  - why: Fast LoadStationary makes weight loads cheap and the small moving tile issues at the 64-cycle turnaround; TensorE is otherwise starved by the 1-column output.
  - when: Single-token matmuls over large weights.
  - fix: nc_matmul(stationary=W_tile[K,128], moving=x[K, n_tokens]); evict transposed output.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki_perf_guide.rst :: Opt #7  [stated, all]
- **op-rmsnorm-vs-layernorm-layout** — For linear -> RMSNorm -> linear chains keep weights stationary and reduce the squared sum across partitions on TensorE; for linear -> LayerNorm swap operands so bn_stats sees features on the free dim.
  - why: bn_stats must reduce along the free dim; RMSNorm's sum can go either way, so choose the layout the following matmul needs ([4H, seq]).
  - when: PF transposes between matmul and normalization.
  - fix: Apply technique 1 (operand swap) for LayerNorm, technique 2 (engine choice) for RMSNorm.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki_perf_guide.rst :: Opt #8 Intermediate Transpose  [stated, all]
- **op-softmax-engine-mapping** — Map softmax as: max-subtract+exp on ScalarE (activation with bias=-max), row sums on VectorE (or activation_reduce), reciprocal scaling on ScalarE, causal mask on GpSimd; on trn3 use VectorE nisa.exponential.
  - why: This split keeps every engine busy in the attention pipeline and uses fused instructions.
  - when: Attention kernels.
  - fix: Pipeline per 128-row tile; avoid TensorE for anything but the two matmuls.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki_perf_guide.rst :: Opt #3; nki/guides/architecture/trainium3_arch.rst :: Fast Exponential Evaluation  [stated, all]
- **op-avoid-tensore-reshapes-in-matmul-kernels** — Avoid TensorE 'alternative uses' (transpose, broadcast, cross-partition sum, shuffles) inside matmul-bound kernels; use them freely in normalization/softmax kernels where TensorE is idle.
  - why: These ops keep TensorE from useful high-throughput work; they are acceptable only when matmuls are not the bottleneck or layout conflicts are unavoidable.
  - when: TensorE transpose share high in a matmul-heavy profile.
  - fix: Move reshapes to VectorE/DMA or fix layouts upstream.
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium_inferentia2_arch.rst :: Alternative Use Case  [stated, all]
- **op-mamba-scan-instruction** — Implement sequential recurrences (Mamba prefix scan, cumulative products) with nisa.tensor_tensor_scan rather than per-timestep tensor_scalar loops.
  - why: The naive implementation issues seq_len dependent one-element instructions (~222 ns each); the scan instruction processes the whole free dim in one pipelined instruction.
  - when: Loop over sequence positions updating a [128,1] state.
  - fix: nisa.tensor_tensor_scan on VectorE (see Fused Mamba tutorial).
  - check (static): flag loops over a sequence dim with single-column tensor_scalar updates.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki_perf_guide.rst :: Opt #5a  [stated, all]
- **op-io-layout-choice** — Choose kernel IO tensor layouts in HBM to match the first consuming instruction's partition requirement and to keep DMAs contiguous; IO transposes are a layout decision, not a hardware necessity.
  - why: A [out_ch, in_ch] weight consumed by nc_matmul as [in_ch, out_ch] needs either a TensorE transpose per tile or a low-bandwidth DMA transpose; delivering it pre-transposed from the framework removes both.
  - when: nl.matmul(transpose_x=False) or nc_transpose right after every load.
  - fix: Expose a transposed weight layout at the framework boundary (weight.t() once) as the tutorial's lhsT does.
  - check (static): flag transposes whose input is a kernel parameter.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki_perf_guide.rst :: Opt #8 IO transpose; nki/guides/tutorials/kernel-optimization.rst :: Starting simple  [stated, all]
- **op-batch-size-ridge-point** — Estimate the batch size at which decode/inference becomes compute-bound as ceil(0.5 x (PeakFLOPS/MemBW) / (model FLOPs per sample / (params x dtype bytes))); below it the kernel is weight-bandwidth bound and DMA rules dominate.
  - why: Arithmetic intensity grows linearly with batch; the roofline ridge is PeakFLOPS/MemBW (BERT-Large bf16 on trn1: batch 2).
  - when: Deciding whether a decode kernel should be tuned for DMA or TensorE.
  - fix: For batch=1 LLM decode assume memory-bound: maximize bytes/partition per DMA, use both LNC cores, keep weights bf16/fp8.
  - numbers: trn1_example = BERT-Large seq128 bf16 -> batch 2 (210 TFLOPS, 820 GB/s)
  - check (simulator): ai_per_sample = flops/(params*bytes); ridge = peak_flops/mem_bw.
  - source: about-neuron/arch/neuron-features/neuroncore-batching.rst :: How to determine the optimal batch-size for inference workloads?  [stated, all]
- **tkg-vs-cte-threshold** — Select the token-generation (TKG) kernel variants when batch*seqlen <= 96; otherwise use the context-encoding (CTE) variants.
  - why: Below ~96 tokens the projection is HBM-bound on weights, so weight-stationary/column-tiled layouts win; above that the PE is better fed with activations stationary.
  - when: Choosing MLP/QKV/attention kernel family.
  - fix: is_tkg = mode in (AUTO, DECODE) and B*S <= 96 and not force_cte_mode
  - numbers: TKG_BS_SEQLEN_THRESHOLD = 96; BS_TILE_SIZE = 128
  - check (static): B*S <= 96 -> tkg
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/core/mlp/mlp_parameters.py is_mlp_tkg  [stated, all]
- **rmsnorm-layout-by-T** — For RMSNorm with T >= 128 tokens use the [T(partition), H(free)] layout with one fused activation_reduce(square, add) per tile; for T < 128 (decode) use [H0, T, H1] with a ones-matrix matmul to finish the reduction across partitions.
  - why: A free-axis reduction is one ScalarE instruction, but it needs tokens on partitions; in decode only a handful of tokens exist, so H is spread over partitions and the cross-partition sum is done on the PE with ones[128,128] @ sq[128,T].
  - when: Any pre-norm in a decode megakernel.
  - fix: nisa.activation(sq, op=nl.square, data=x[128,T,H1]); nisa.tensor_reduce(red, nl.add, sq, axis=2); nisa.nc_matmul(dst=psum, stationary=ones[128,128], moving=red[128,T]); nisa.activation(red, op=nl.rsqrt, data=psum, scale=1/H, bias=eps_sb)
  - numbers: T switch = 128; T_FULL_TILE_SIZE = 512
  - check (static): rmsnorm with T<128 using free-axis-only reduction
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/core/mlp/mlp_tkg/mlp_tkg_rmsnorm.py rmsnorm_tkg/_rmsnorm_tkg_ht/_rmsnorm_tkg_th  [stated, all]
- **rope-contiguous-half-layout** — Store RoPE channels in contiguous [first_half | second_half] order on the partition axis so rotate-half is two partition-sliced tensor_tensor ops; convert interleaved [even,odd,...] layouts with stride-2 DMA slices, or a permutation matmul only when B*heads*S <= 512.
  - why: Contiguous halves let x[:half] and x[half:] be addressed as partition ranges; interleaved layouts need a gather. The matmul relayout is limited by gemm_moving_fmax.
  - when: Q/K RoPE in decode.
  - fix: nisa.dma_copy(dst=x_sb[:half], src=x.slice(0,0,d,2)); nisa.dma_copy(dst=x_sb[half:], src=x.slice(0,1,d,2))  # interleaved->contiguous on load
  - numbers: gemm_moving_fmax = 512
  - check (static): RoPE on interleaved layout with B*heads*S > 512 using matmul relayout
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/core/embeddings/rope.py RoPE (is_dma_relayout / is_relayout_in_sbuf)  [stated, all]
- **rope-via-rotation-matrix-on-pe** — Implement rotate-half as a single nc_matmul against a signed block-circulant permutation matrix built from the shared identity when the Vector/Scalar engines are the bottleneck.
  - why: The PE is often idle in decode; a [128,128] stationary rotation matrix performs the shift and negation in one instruction. nc_matmul applies stationary.T, so build the inverse shift.
  - when: Fused RoPE inside attention/QKV where DVE/ACT are saturated.
  - fix: rot = build_rotation_matrix(128, 1, shifts=64, dtype=nl.float16, negate=True); nisa.nc_matmul(psum, stationary=rot, moving=x)
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/core/utils/rotation_matrix.py build_rotation_matrix  [stated, all]
- **qk-swap-path-disabled** — Do not rely on the experimental QK-swap (Q-stationary, column-tiled) MM1 path; it is hard-gated off (`return False`) due to OOB errors, and only applied to block KV with curr_sprior >= 1024 and 4 < s_active_qh <= 128.
  - why: Production kernels keep K stationary; the swap variant is still being validated.
  - when: Considering Q-stationary scores for batch>1 decode.
  - fix: is_qk_swapped(...) -> False; keep K stationary
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/core/attention/attention_tkg_utils.py is_qk_swapped (TODO: remove this gate)  [stated, trn2]
- **scan-op-for-recurrences** — Express first-order linear recurrences with nisa.tensor_tensor_scan(op0=multiply, op1=add, initial=carry) and carry the last column into the next chunk's initial.
  - why: A native scan instruction replaces a serial loop over positions.
  - when: SSM / cumulative products along the free axis.
  - fix: nisa.tensor_tensor_scan(dst=res, data0=A, data1=Bu, initial=scan_init, op0=nl.multiply, op1=nl.add); nisa.tensor_copy(scan_init, res[:, -1:])
  - source: aws-neuron/nki-samples:src/nki_samples/tutorials/fused_mamba/mamba_nki_kernels.py  [stated, all]
- **interp-advanced-indexing-affine-mgrid** — Express bilinear/trilinear 2x upsampling as a few affine-index gathers over the loaded tile (nl.mgrid with i_dst = 2*i_y+1+i_x and i_src = i_y + i_x / i_y + (1-i_x)) combined in one weighted expression, with separate expressions for faces/edges/corners.
  - why: Affine index expressions over a SBUF tile lower to strided access patterns (no indirect DMA); each neighbour read is a strided view and the weighted sum is a handful of VectorE ops per chunk.
  - when: Upsampling / stencil ops where the compiler handles gather poorly.
  - fix: i_p,i_hx,i_wx,i_hy,i_wy = nl.mgrid[0:128,0:2,0:2,0:h-1,0:w-1]; out[i_p, 2*i_hy+1+i_hx, 2*i_wy+1+i_wx] = 9/16*in[i_p,i_hy+i_hx,i_wy+i_wx] + 3/16*in[...] + 3/16*in[...] + 1/16*in[...]
  - numbers: weights 2x align_corners=False = 9/16,3/16,3/16,1/16
  - source: aws-neuron/nki-samples:contributed/interpolate_bilinear_fwd.py, interpolate_trilinear_fwd.py (old API)  [stated, all]
- **pool-via-strided-ap-view-reduce** — Implement pooling/windowed reductions as a strided .ap() view that exposes the window dims last, followed by one nl.sum/nl.max over those axes, not loop-based gathers.
  - why: A single instruction with a multi-dim access pattern replaces k*k shifted copies.
  - when: avg/max pool, windowed stats.
  - fix: pool_view = in_tile.ap([[H*W, P],[k*W, H//k],[k, W//k],[W, k],[1, k]]); nl.sum(pool_view, axis=[3,4])
  - source: aws-neuron/nki-samples:src/nki_samples/tutorials/average_pool2d/average_pool2d_nki_kernels.py; contributed/maxpooling.py  [stated, all]
- **iota-for-index-generation** — Generate index/offset vectors on-chip with nisa.iota(pattern, offset, channel_multiplier) rather than loading them from HBM.
  - why: Cheap VectorE instruction; avoids a DMA and keeps indices in the right dtype (uint32 for DMA, fp32 for iota-based masks).
  - when: Batch offsets, parity masks, position-id masks.
  - fix: nisa.iota(ones_tile, [[0,1]], offset=1); even idx: odd partitions get 0xFFFFFFFF -> OOB skip
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/experimental/transformer/attention_block_tkg.py ~2127, 2485-2493; attention_tkg.py ~522 (int32 for DMA, fp32 for iota)  [stated, all]
- **transpose2d-element-copies-are-slow** — Avoid implementing free-dim permutations as per-element nisa.tensor_copy loops (as in the transpose2d tutorial); use a strided .ap() view in a single tensor_copy or a dma_copy with transposing pattern.
  - why: The element-copy loop emits F1*F2 instructions; one AP-based copy does it in a single instruction.
  - when: Any [P, F1, F2] -> [P, F2, F1] swap.
  - fix: nisa.tensor_copy(dst=out, src=in_tile.ap([[F1*F2,P],[1,F2],[F2,F1]]))
  - check (static): tensor_copy with nl.ds(...,1) inside nested affine loops
  - source: aws-neuron/nki-samples:src/nki_samples/tutorials/transpose2d/transpose2d_nki_kernels.py (illustrative); mlp_tkg_utils.transpose_store_sbuf_copy  [inferred, all]
- **flat-cache-update-path-selection** — Choose the KV-cache update path by shape: block cache -> vectorised scatter; S_tkg==1 and B>1 (and not transposed K or B>16) -> batched vector DMA; else per-batch scalar DMA.
  - why: Vector DGE with indirect addressing amortises descriptor cost over the batch but is buggy for S_tkg>1.
  - when: KV cache write in decode.
  - fix: if is_block_kv: _update_block_cache(...) elif S_tkg==1 and B>1 and (not K_cache_transposed or B>16): _update_flat_cache_batched(...) else: _update_flat_cache(...)
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/experimental/transformer/attention_block_tkg.py ~2015-2040  [stated, all]
- **psum-accumulation-beats-vector-accumulation** — Accumulate partial matmul products in PSUM via the tensor engine rather than summing partial results on the vector engine with tensor_tensor.
  - why: PSUM accumulation is done in FP32 by the PE array with very low overhead; VectorE tensor_tensor accumulation is significantly slower and adds PSUM->SBUF traffic per partial.
  - when: A pattern of nc_matmul into fresh PSUM per K tile followed by tensor_tensor(op=nl.add) to combine.
  - fix: Reuse one PSUM dst across K tiles with accumulate=(k_idx > 0).

- **pretranspose-weights-offline** — Supply matmul operands already in [K, M] (lhsT) layout instead of transposing tiles on-device with nc_transpose.
  - why: nc_transpose executes as TRANSPOSE MATMUL instructions that consume tensor engine FLOPs without useful work; one transpose per matmul added 11.1% of hardware FLOPs and 24% of runtime in the worked example.
  - when: Profile gap compute_bound_ideal_flops -> compute_bound_ideal_useful_flops > 0, or Summary.transpose_flops > 0; code calls nc_transpose inside the matmul loop.
  - fix: Pre-transpose weights at load time (or ask for the transposed layout) and pass lhsT[K, M] directly as the stationary operand.
  - numbers: example_transpose_overhead = 11.1% of hw_flops, 27.3 us at peak, 24% total time
  - check (profile): count Instruction rows with tensor_instruction_type == 'TRANSPOSE'; report transpose_flops / hw_flops per source line
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-profile-querying/references/investigations/redundant_te_transposes.md :: Worked example  [stated, all]
- **small-relayout-via-permutation-matmul** — For interleaved<->contiguous relayouts of tensors whose flattened free size fits nl.tile_size.gemm_moving_fmax, use a permutation-matrix matmul in SBUF instead of strided DMA.
  - why: A permutation matmul runs at TE speed on data already in SBUF; strided DMA pays HBM descriptor overhead. For larger tensors only strided DMA fits.
  - when: RoPE-style even/odd interleave with B*n_heads*S <= gemm_moving_fmax (~512).
  - fix: Build perm_matrix [d_head, d_head] via .ap() patterns ([[d_head,d_head],[1,2],[2,half_d]]) and compute nc_matmul(perm, x).
  - numbers: threshold = nl.tile_size.gemm_moving_fmax (~512 elements)
  - check (static): if relayout tensor free size <= gemm_moving_fmax -> suggest permutation matmul else strided DMA
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-writing/references/transpose-and-layout.md :: Alternative: SBUF Relayout with MatMul  [stated, all]
- **dma-transpose-over-copy-plus-nc-transpose** — For HBM->SBUF loads that need a transposed layout, use nisa.dma_transpose in one step rather than dma_copy followed by nc_transpose.
  - why: dma_transpose performs the transpose inside the DMA engine, saving tensor-engine TRANSPOSE matmuls and a PSUM round trip; note transposed DMA loads are themselves less efficient than plain loads.
  - when: dma_copy immediately followed by nc_transpose of the same tile in the load path.
  - fix: nisa.dma_transpose(dst=sbuf[0:p, 0:f], src=hbm[0:f, 0:p]) with dst rank exactly matching the transposed src rank (NKI 0.4.0).
  - check (static): flag nc_transpose whose data was produced solely by a preceding dma_copy from HBM
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-writing/references/indexing-patterns.md :: dma_transpose specific; /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-profile-querying/references/investigations/dma_efficiency.md :: Source-line attribution  [stated, all]
- **fuse-scale-bias-into-activation** — Fold a preceding multiply and/or add into nisa.activation via scale= and bias= (exp(x*s), sigmoid(x+b), tanh(x*s+b)) instead of a separate tensor_scalar.
  - why: ScalarE applies a pipelined multiply-add before the nonlinear function, so two ops cost one instruction; the separate form is 2x slower.
  - when: tensor_scalar(multiply/add) whose result feeds only an activation.
  - fix: nisa.activation(dst=out, op=nl.exp, data=x, scale=s, bias=b).
  - numbers: speedup = 2x (one instruction instead of two)
  - check (static): flag tensor_scalar(op0 in {multiply, add}) whose sole consumer is nisa.activation on the same tile
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-writing/references/common-patterns.md :: Fused Operations on ScalarE  [stated, all]
- **tensor-tensor-scan-for-recurrences** — Implement cumsum, cumprod, RNN-style and SSM recurrences with a single nisa.tensor_tensor_scan per tile and carry the last column as initial= to the next tile, instead of a sequential loop over elements.
  - why: An explicit loop emits seq_len instructions each on a 1-element-per-partition tile with data dependencies, so static instruction overhead dominates; the scan instruction caches intermediates inside VectorE.
  - when: for i in nl.sequential_range(seq_len): out[:, i] = f(out[:, i-1], x[:, i]).
  - fix: nisa.tensor_tensor_scan(dst, data0, data1, initial, op0=nl.multiply, op1=nl.add) computing out[i] = op0(data0[i], out[i-1]) op1 data1[i]; cumsum uses data0=ones, cumprod uses data1=zeros, initial=1.
  - check (static): flag sequential_range loops whose body reads dst[:, i-1] and writes dst[:, i]
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-writing/references/common-patterns.md :: Sequential Operations & Associative Scan  [stated, all]
- **broadcast-partition0-with-stream-shuffle** — Replicate a bias/scale that lives in partition 0 to all 128 partitions with stream_shuffle_broadcast (nc_stream_shuffle); use tp_broadcast only for the rare column-vector (P) to row (F) broadcast.
  - why: There is no cross-partition broadcast via indexing; the stream-shuffle engine path moves a partition-0 row to every PE lane without a DMA round trip.
  - when: A 1-D parameter loaded into one partition that must be applied to every row of a [128, F] tile.
  - fix: stream_shuffle_broadcast(src, dst) before the tensor_tensor/activation that consumes it.
  - check (static): flag tensor_tensor where one operand has shape[0]==1 and the other shape[0]==128 without a broadcast view
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-writing/SKILL.md :: Utility Selection Guide (stream_shuffle_broadcast, tp_broadcast)  [stated, all]
- **zero-copy-views-instead-of-tensor-copy-chains** — Express reshapes, permutes of free dims, free-dim broadcasts (stride 0) and strided slices as zero-copy views (NkiTensor methods, TensorView, or .ap()) rather than chains of nisa.tensor_copy.
  - why: Views are compile-time stride computations with no runtime cost; each tensor_copy is a full vector-engine pass over the tile and consumes SBUF.
  - when: tensor_copy used only to change shape/layout of free dims, or to materialize a broadcast.
  - fix: TensorView(x).reshape_dim(1,[F1,F2]).permute([0,2,1]).get_view(); src.ap(pattern=[[1,128],[0,512]]) for a free-dim broadcast; TensorView(cos).expand_dim(2).broadcast(2, n_heads).

  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-writing/references/transpose-and-layout.md :: Anti-pattern 3: Excessive Data Movement; Example 1: Zero-Stride Broadcast  [stated, all]
- **bn-stats-for-normalization** — Compute mean/variance for layernorm-style ops with nisa.bn_stats over chunks of the free dim rather than separate reduce passes.
  - why: bn_stats produces per-partition statistics in one vector-engine pass; manual sum and sum-of-squares need two reductions plus elementwise squares.
  - when: LayerNorm / RMSNorm / batchnorm kernels doing tensor_reduce twice per row.
  - fix: nisa.bn_stats(dst=stats[0:p, nl.ds(i*DST_SIZE, DST_SIZE)], data=x[0:p, nl.ds(off, sz)]) per chunk, then aggregate.
  - check (static): flag pair of tensor_reduce(add) over x and over x*x feeding a variance computation
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-writing/references/indexing-patterns.md :: 4. nl.ds() for Dynamic Slices (bn_stats example)  [inferred, all]
- **prefer-fused-reduce-variants** — Prefer fused ISA ops (activation_reduce, tensor_scalar_reduce, tensor_scalar_cumulative, activate2) over an elementwise op followed by a separate tensor_reduce when the pattern matches.
  - why: Each fused instruction does the elementwise work and the reduction in one engine pass, halving vector/scalar engine time and instruction count (e.g. softmax exp + row sum).
  - when: nisa.activation followed immediately by tensor_reduce on its output along the free axis.
  - fix: nisa.activation_reduce(...) producing both the activated tile and the row reduction.
  - check (static): flag activation/tensor_scalar whose output feeds tensor_reduce with no other consumer
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/neuron_agentic_development/artifacts/skills/neuron-nki-writing/SKILL.md :: API features documented in /neuron-nki-docs (ops list supporting .indirect)  [inferred, all]
- **transpose-kind-selects-instruction** — Use nisa.nc_transpose for a partition<->free transpose and an access-pattern copy (nisa.tensor_copy or dma_copy with rearranged free indices) for a free<->free transpose.
  - why: Only TensorE (nc_transpose) can move data across partitions; permuting two free axes is just a different per-partition address pattern.
  - when: Any transpose request.
  - fix: P<->F: nisa.nc_transpose(dst, data). F1<->F2: copy in_tile[P, F1, F2] into out_tile[P, F2, F1] via strided indexing.
  - check (static): If permutation moves dim0 -> require nc_transpose; else emit tensor_copy with permuted view.
  - source: nki/guides/tutorials/transpose2d.rst :: Transpose2D; nki/get-started/about/indexing-overview.rst :: Case #2  [stated, all]
- **tensor-scalar-2x-faster-than-tensor-tensor-fp32** — Prefer nisa.tensor_scalar over nisa.tensor_tensor when one operand is a per-partition scalar, because tensor_tensor is 2x slower for FP32.
  - why: tensor_tensor reads two full tiles and only runs on VectorE; tensor_scalar reads one tile plus a scalar and can run on VectorE or ScalarE.
  - when: Element-wise op where one operand has free size 1.
  - fix: nisa.tensor_scalar(data=x, op0=nl.multiply, operand0=vec[:,0:1]).
  - numbers: tensor_tensor_vs_tensor_scalar_fp32 = 2x slower
  - check (static): tensor_tensor whose data2 has shape (P,1) or is a broadcast -> replace.
  - source: nki/guides/tutorials/fused_mamba.rst :: Step 1  [stated, all]
- **tensor-scalar-dual-op** — Use the op0/op1 pair of nisa.tensor_scalar to perform two pipelined scalar ops (e.g. multiply then add) at the cost of one instruction.
  - why: tensor_scalar supports two operators in a pipelined fashion within one instruction.
  - when: mul followed by add with per-partition scalars.
  - fix: nisa.tensor_scalar(x, op0=nl.multiply, operand0=a, op1=nl.add, operand1=b)
  - numbers: speedup = ~2x vs two instructions
  - check (static): Two consecutive tensor_scalar on the same tile -> merge.
  - source: nki/guides/tutorials/fused_mamba.rst :: Step 4  [stated, all]
- **use-tensor-tensor-scan-for-recurrence** — Implement first-order recurrences (x[t] = a[t]*x[t-1] + b[t]) with a single nisa.tensor_tensor_scan instead of a seq_len-long chain of dependent single-column instructions.
  - why: Each dependent tensor_scalar on a [P,1] tile pays the fixed instruction overhead; tensor_tensor_scan keeps the running state inside VectorE.
  - when: A sequential_range loop over the free dim with a loop-carried column dependency.
  - fix: scan = nisa.tensor_tensor_scan(deltaA, deltaBu, initial=0, op0=nl.multiply, op1=nl.add)
  - check (static): Loop over free index with body reading out[:, i] and writing out[:, i+1] -> suggest tensor_tensor_scan.
  - source: nki/guides/tutorials/fused_mamba.rst :: Step 4  [stated, all]
- **mlp-tkg-vs-cte-threshold** — Use (or expect) the MLP TKG path when batch_size x sequence_length <= 96 and the CTE path otherwise; override with mode=ComputationMode.DECODE/PREFILL or force_cte_mode.
  - why: The library dispatches on B*S; TKG is tuned for tiny token counts (column tiling, SBUF output, FP8), CTE for throughput.
  - when: Calling nkilib mlp or designing a decode MLP.
  - fix: mlp(..., mode=ComputationMode.AUTO)  # TKG iff B*S <= 96
  - numbers: tkg_threshold = B*S <= 96
  - check (static): B*S <= 96 -> TKG features allowed.
  - source: nki/library/api/mlp.rst :: Notes  [stated, all]
- **fused-residual-add-in-qkv** — Fuse the residual stream into the next projection (input + mlp_prev + attention_prev) instead of a separate add kernel.
  - why: qkv's fused_residual_add consumes both previous outputs during its input load.
  - when: Transformer layer with residual connections.
  - fix: qkv(..., fused_residual_add=True, mlp_prev=..., attention_prev=...)
  - source: nki/library/api/qkv.rst :: Fused Operations Support  [stated, all]
- **attention-tkg-regime** — Use attention_tkg for decode with s_active <= 7 and d_head <= 128, and attention_cte for prefill with sequence length > 256.
  - why: attention_tkg is tuned for tiny active sequences against large KV caches; attention_cte for long Q/K sequences with flash-style sectioning.
  - when: Choosing the library attention kernel.
  - fix: attention_tkg(q,k_active,v_active,k_prior,v_prior,mask,out,cfg,sbm) or attention_cte(q,k,v,...)
  - numbers: tkg_s_active_max = 7; cte_seq_min = 256; d_head_max = 128
  - check (static): s_active<=7 -> tkg; seqlen>256 -> cte.
  - source: nki/library/api/attention-tkg.rst :: Constraints; nki/library/api/attention-cte.rst :: Background  [stated, all]
- **rope-layout-conversion-strategy** — Convert interleaved RoPE layout to contiguous with a permutation-matrix matmul in SBUF only when B*n_heads*S <= 512 (gemm_moving_fmax); otherwise use strided DMA with step=2.
  - why: The SBUF matmul path needs the whole free extent in one moving tile; strided DMA works for any size.
  - when: Model weights use interleaved (even/odd) RoPE.
  - fix: RoPE(x, cos, sin, contiguous_layout=False, relayout_in_sbuf=(B*n_heads*S<=512))
  - numbers: sbuf_relayout_max = B*n_heads*S<=512
  - check (static): relayout_in_sbuf and B*n_heads*S>512 -> error.
  - source: nki/library/api/rope.rst :: Layout Conversion Strategies  [stated, all]
- **stream-shuffle-broadcast-for-bias** — Broadcast a [1,H] bias across partitions with stream_shuffle_broadcast (DVE) by default, or with a TensorE ones-matmul when TensorE is idle.
  - why: Partition broadcast needs a hardware shuffle or a matmul; the library offers both (use_PE_broadcast_w_bias / use_pe_broadcast).
  - when: Adding bias/gamma rows to a [128, H] tile.
  - fix: nkilib stream_shuffle_broadcast(bias) or matmul(ones[1,128].T, bias[1,H]).
  - source: nki/library/api/output-projection-cte.rst :: Stream Shuffle Broadcast; nki/library/api/router-topk.rst :: Bias Broadcasting  [stated, all]
- **skip-output-normalization-for-ring** — When a caller (e.g. ring attention) will merge partial softmax results, request unnormalized output plus raw denominators (skip_output_normalization=True with cache_softmax=True) and normalize once at the end.
  - why: Avoids repeated 1/S normalization per step.
  - when: Context-parallel attention across ranks.
  - fix: attention_cte(..., cache_softmax=True, skip_output_normalization=True)
  - source: nki/library/api/attention-cte.rst :: skip_output_normalization  [stated, all]
- **activation-reduce-for-sum-of-squares** — Compute sum(x^2) with nisa.activation_reduce (square + reduce-add in one ScalarE instruction) rather than a square followed by a separate reduce.
  - why: The reduce-add comes for free with the activation.
  - when: RMSNorm, L2 norm, variance.
  - fix: nisa.activation_reduce(op=nl.square, data=x, reduce_op=nl.add, reduce_res=ss)
  - check (static): activation(square) followed by tensor_reduce(add) on same tile -> fuse.
  - source: nki/library/specs/design-rmsnorm-quant.rst :: activation_reduce; nki/library/api/foreach-norm.rst  [stated, all]
- **moe-tkg-regime** — Use moe_tkg when T = batch*seq <= 128 (except MX all-expert mode) and moe_cte with blockwise matmul when T > 128.
  - why: TKG processes all tokens on one partition tile; CTE groups tokens into expert blocks.
  - when: MoE layer in decode vs prefill.
  - fix: moe_tkg(hidden[T,H] or SBUF [H0,T,H1], ..., output_in_sbuf=True)
  - numbers: tkg_T_max = 128
  - check (static): T<=128 -> tkg.
  - source: nki/library/api/moe-tkg.rst :: Constraints; nki/library/api/moe-cte.rst :: Background  [stated, all]

## DMA: payload size, descriptors, coalescing (92)

- **dma-transpose-dtype-and-width** — Only dma_transpose tensors whose dtype is 2 bytes and whose last dim is <= 128, with dst in SBUF and dst.dtype == src.dtype.
  - why: The DMA transpose path (HWDGE or gather-transpose) moves 2-byte elements and is limited to 128 output partitions.
  - when: dma_transpose on fp32/int8 tensors or on src.shape[-1] > 128.
  - fix: Cast to bf16/fp16 before transposing, or tile the last dim to <=128; for fp32 use Tensor Engine transpose.
  - numbers: dtype_size = 2 bytes; last_dim_max = 128
  - check (static): dma_transpose: itemsize(src.dtype)==2 and src.shape[-1]<=128 and buffer(dst)==sbuf and dst.dtype==src.dtype
  - source: nki.isa.dma_transpose docstring, Direct and Indirect constraints  [stated, all]
- **dma-transpose-hwdge-shape-rules** — For HWDGE dma_transpose use src.shape[0]==16 for 2-D input, or shape[0] in {1,2,4,8,16} with (shape[0]*shape[-2]) % 16 == 0 for 3-D/4-D input.
  - why: The hardware descriptor generator transposes in 16-row blocks.
  - when: 2-D src with 128 rows passed to dma_transpose with dge_mode=hwdge.
  - fix: Reshape to a 3-D view (16, rows/16, cols) or let dge_mode=unknown choose; for arbitrary shapes use PE transpose.
  - numbers: block_rows = 16
  - check (static): dma_transpose(dge_mode in {hwdge,unknown}): ndim==2 -> shape[0]==16; ndim in {3,4} -> shape[0] in {1,2,4,8,16} and shape[0]*shape[-2]%16==0
  - source: nki.isa.dma_transpose docstring, DMA Direct Transpose Constraints  [stated, trn2]
- **dma-transpose-axes-and-rank** — Pass axes as exactly (1,0), (2,1,0) or (3,1,2,0) and give dst the same rank as src with the transposed shape.
  - why: Only these permutations are implemented; since NKI 0.4.0 a lower-rank dst is an assertion error instead of being silently padded.
  - when: dst 3-D vs src 4-D, or axes=(0,2,1).
  - fix: Match dst rank to src (e.g. (128,1,1,4096) for a 4-D src) or use a 3-D src with axes=(2,1,0).
  - check (static): dma_transpose: axes in allowed set and dst.ndim==src.ndim and dst.shape==permute(src.shape,axes)
  - source: nki.isa.dma_transpose docstring; migration/index.rst section 0.3->0.4 dma_transpose  [stated, all]
- **dma-transpose-indirect-rules** — For indirect (gather) dma_transpose on trn2+: src in HBM with shape[0] % 16 == 0, uint32 indices in SBUF with shape[0] in [16,128] divisible by 16 (exactly 128 when indices.shape[1] > 1), dge_mode swdge/unknown.
  - why: It lowers to a software-DGE dma_gather_transpose that gathers rows by index then transposes.
  - when: Indices in HBM, int32 indices, or 4-D src where both middle dims exceed 1.
  - fix: Stage indices as nl.uint32 SBUF (128,N); ensure indices.shape[0]*indices.shape[1] >= src.shape[0].
  - check (static): dma_transpose with indices: indices.dtype==uint32 and buffer(indices)==sbuf and 16<=indices.shape[0]<=128 and %16==0 and buffer(src)==hbm
  - source: nki.isa.dma_transpose docstring, DMA Indirect Transpose Constraints  [stated, trn2]
- **dma-copy-no-psum-source** — Never dma_copy directly out of PSUM; copy PSUM to SBUF with tensor_copy/activation first.
  - why: Since NKI 0.3.0 DMA engines cannot read PSUM; the DMA path only connects HBM and SBUF.
  - when: nisa.dma_copy(dst=hbm, src=psum_tile) after a matmul.
  - fix: sb = nl.ndarray(shape, dtype, buffer=nl.sbuf); nisa.tensor_copy(dst=sb, src=psum); nisa.dma_copy(dst=hbm, src=sb).
  - check (static): dma_copy: buffer(src) != psum and buffer(dst) != psum
  - source: migration/index.rst section 'nisa.dma_copy - reading from PSUM'; nki.isa.dma_copy docstring Memory types  [stated, all]
- **dma-copy-element-count-match** — Make src and dst of dma_copy have identical total element counts (shapes may differ).
  - why: DMA moves a flat stream of elements described by two access patterns; mismatched counts are rejected.
  - when: Copying a (128,512) tile into a (128,256) destination slice.
  - fix: Slice both sides to the same count; use .ap()/reshape views for layout changes.
  - check (static): dma_copy: prod(src.shape)==prod(dst.shape)
  - source: nki.isa.dma_copy docstring, section Tile size  [stated, all]
- **dma-dge-mode-selection** — Choose dge_mode deliberately: none (runtime pre-generated descriptors, static addresses only), swdge (GpSimd generates, needed for gather/scatter), hwdge (Sync/Scalar sequencer, trn2+, dynamic start address).
  - why: Dynamic (register/SBUF-dependent) addresses cannot use pre-generated descriptors; only swdge supports per-partition vector indices; hwdge costs no GpSimd time.
  - when: Indirect dma_copy with dge_mode=none, or hwdge requested on trn1.
  - fix: Leave dge_mode=unknown unless profiling shows GpSimd is a bottleneck, then move static/scalar-offset copies to hwdge with engine=sync or scalar.
  - check (static): dma_copy: vector_offset used -> dge_mode in {swdge,unknown}; hwdge -> nc_version>=3
  - source: nki.isa.dma_copy docstring, DGE modes paragraph and params  [stated, all]
- **dma-oob-mode-skip-for-dynamic** — Set oob_mode=nisa.oob_mode.skip on indirect dma_copy/dma_compute/dma_transpose when indices may legitimately exceed bounds (e.g. padded expert tables).
  - why: Dynamic DMAs enable bounds checking; the default oob_mode.error raises a runtime error instead of silently skipping.
  - when: MoE/gather kernels failing at runtime with OOB DMA errors.
  - fix: Add oob_mode=nisa.oob_mode.skip, or clamp indices before the copy.
  - source: nki.isa.dma_copy docstring, param oob_mode  [stated, all]
- **dma-vector-offset-rules** — For gather/scatter dma_copy use .ap(pattern, vector_offset=idx, indirect_dim=0) on the HBM tensor, with idx an SBUF (P,1) tensor; only indirect_dim=0 is supported.
  - why: Vector indirection gives each of the P partitions its own row index; the stride on the indirect dim is taken from the base tensor shape, not the pattern.
  - when: vector_offset applied to an SBUF tensor, idx in HBM, or indirect_dim=1.
  - fix: Load indices into SBUF (P,1) int32/uint32 first; put the indirected tensor (HBM) on the side with .ap(); set pattern stride of dim 0 to prod(base.shape[1:]).
  - check (static): ap(vector_offset=...): buffer(self)==hbm and buffer(vector_offset)==sbuf and vector_offset.shape[1]==1 and indirect_dim==0
  - source: nki.isa.dma_copy docstring, Indirect addressing; migration/index.rst 'Vector dynamic access'  [stated, all]
- **dma-scalar-offset-semantics** — For a dynamic uniform offset use .ap(pattern, scalar_offset=reg_or_1x1_sbuf, indirect_dim=N); the element offset added is scalar_offset * prod(base.shape[N+1:]).
  - why: indirect_dim is relative to the base tensor, not the pattern; the scalar may be a 1x1 SBUF tensor or a VirtualRegister.
  - when: Off-by-stride bugs when the pattern shape differs from the base shape.
  - fix: Compute offsets against base tensor shape; vector_offset and scalar_offset are mutually exclusive.
  - check (static): ap(): not (scalar_offset and vector_offset)
  - source: nki.isa.dma_copy docstring; migration/index.rst 'Scalar dynamic access'  [stated, all]
- **dma-compute-constraints** — Use dma_compute only with reduce_op=nl.add, scales all 1.0/None, <= 16 sources of identical element count, and for scatter/gather RMW exactly 2 sources with unique_indices=True.
  - why: Current DMA compute logic supports only summation; RMW uses SW DGE while plain dma_compute uses static DMA (compiler assigns).
  - when: dma_compute with nl.maximum, non-unit scales, or 3 sources with vector_offset.
  - fix: Pre-scale in SBUF with tensor_scalar; split into pairwise adds.
  - numbers: max_srcs = 16
  - check (static): dma_compute: reduce_op==add and all(s==1.0) and len(srcs)<=16 and (vector_offset present -> len(srcs)==2 and unique_indices)
  - source: nki.isa.dma_compute docstring  [stated, all]
- **dma-4kib-per-partition-target** — Size every HBM<->SBUF DMA so each partition moves at least 2 KiB of contiguous data, targeting 4 KiB or more.
  - why: Each DMA transfer pays fixed descriptor-setup, synchronization and semaphore-to-start costs; below ~2 KiB per partition the DMA packet rate, not HBM bandwidth, limits throughput. At 4096 free bytes the DMA curve nearly saturates.
  - when: A dma_copy/nl.load whose free-dim bytes per partition are < 2048 (fp32 < 512 elems, bf16 < 1024 elems, fp8 < 2048 elems).
  - fix: Widen the free dimension of the DMA tile (coalesce adjacent sub-tiles into one transfer) until bytes/partition >= 4096.
  - numbers: min_recommended_bytes_per_partition = 2048 B; saturation_bytes_per_partition = 4096 B; fp32_min_free = 512 elements; bf16_fp16_min_free = 1024 elements; fp8_min_free = 2048 elements
  - check (static): for each dma op: bytes_per_partition = prod(free_shape)*dtype_bytes; flag if < 2048; warn if < 4096.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dma-bandwidth-guide.rst :: Bandwidth vs. Payload Size; nki/get-started/about/nki-dma-overview.rst :: Performance Considerations  [stated, all]
- **dma-use-all-128-partitions** — Spread every DMA across all 128 SBUF partitions so all 16 DMA engines participate.
  - why: Each DMA engine serves a fixed group of 8 SBUF partitions (128/16); a transfer touching only P partitions uses ceil(P/8) engines. A [4,4096] bf16 load used 1 engine and took 1416 ns for 32 KiB while 15 engines idled.
  - when: dma_copy whose SBUF-side partition count is far below 128 (e.g. 4, 16, 32).
  - fix: Reshape the transfer so the partition dimension is 128 (e.g. view [4,4096] as [128,128]) or batch several small tensors into one 128-partition tile.
  - numbers: dma_engines_per_core = 16; partitions_per_dma_engine = 8; example_1_engine_32KiB_latency = 1416 ns
  - check (static): for each dma op touching SBUF: engines_used = ceil(P/8); flag if P < 128 and the transfer is on the critical path.
  - source: nki/get-started/about/nki-dma-overview.rst :: Example 1 / Example 2; nki/deep-dives/nki-dma-bandwidth-guide.rst :: Practical Guidance  [stated, all]
- **dma-engine-bandwidth-table** — Budget memory-bound kernels against per-core DMA bandwidth: 16 engines x 23 B/ns = 368 GB/s on Trainium2.
  - why: Each NeuronCore is paired with 16 DMA engines; each engine moves one transfer at a time at a fixed peak rate (17 B/ns trn1, 23 B/ns trn2, 33 B/ns trn3). Per-engine theoretical peak is also quoted as 27.2 GB/s (v2/v3) and 38.4 GB/s (v4).
  - when: Estimating the lower bound of a weight-streaming kernel's runtime, or checking achieved MBU.
  - fix: Runtime_lower_bound = bytes_moved / 368e9 on trn2 per core; if achieved is far above this, apply the payload-size and partition rules.
  - numbers: trn1_bw_per_engine = 17 B/ns; trn1_aggregate = 272 GB/s; trn2_bw_per_engine = 23 B/ns; trn2_aggregate = 368 GB/s; trn3_bw_per_engine = 33 B/ns; trn3_aggregate = 528 GB/s; v2_v3_theoretical_per_engine = 27.2 GB/s; v4_theoretical_per_engine = 38.4 GB/s
  - check (simulator): runtime_lb = total_dma_bytes / (16*23e9); report achieved/lb ratio.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dma-bandwidth-guide.rst :: Why Large Contiguous DMA Payloads Are Required; nki/get-started/about/nki-dma-overview.rst :: Basic DMA Capabilities / Performance Considerations  [stated, all]
- **dma-transfer-size-32kib** — Make each DMA transfer (per engine) at least 32 KiB; a 128x1024 fp32 load maps to 16 transfers of 32 KiB each.
  - why: The compiler splits one nl.load into up to 16 DMA transfers (one per engine), each a scatter-gather list of 8 partition buffers. Transfer-level overhead is amortized only when each transfer is large; 32 B transfers seen in profiles were overhead-dominated.
  - when: Profile DMA-per-engine view shows gaps longer than active bars, or hover shows tiny transfer sizes (e.g. 32 B).
  - fix: Load [128, 1024] fp32 (or equivalent bytes) per nl.load; beyond 1024 fp32 elements per partition returns diminish and pipelining suffers.
  - numbers: ideal_transfer_size = >= 32 KiB; ideal_free_dim_fp32 = 1024 elements; good_dma_utilization_example = 85%
  - check (static): transfer_bytes = (P/16)*free_bytes; flag if < 32768.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki_perf_guide.rst :: Opt #9: Perform sufficiently large DMA transfers  [stated, trn1]
- **dma-per-transfer-overhead-1300ns** — Treat every DMA transfer as costing ~1300 ns of cross-engine synchronization before data moves; amortize it with large payloads.
  - why: Each DMA transfer involves descriptor setup, synchronization and semaphore-to-start latency (~1300 ns cross-engine). Small transfers make the engine spend more time on overhead than data.
  - when: Many small DMAs in the inner loop; DMA active time high but MBU < 60%.
  - fix: Coalesce into fewer, larger DMAs; prefetch a block ahead so the fixed latency overlaps compute.
  - numbers: semaphore_to_start_latency = ~1300 ns (cross-engine)
  - check (simulator): per_dma_cost = 1300ns + bytes/(23 B/ns); flag loops where overhead term > 30% of total.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dma-bandwidth-guide.rst :: Why Large Contiguous DMA Payloads Are Required  [stated, all]
- **dma-coalesce-adjacent-transfers** — Issue one DMA covering multiple logical sub-tiles instead of many DMAs to adjacent addresses.
  - why: Per-packet overhead is fixed per DMA; one large transfer to contiguous addresses fills the engine pipelines, many small ones do not.
  - when: A loop issuing dma_copy per 128x128 tile where the tiles are contiguous in HBM.
  - fix: Allocate an SBUF tile [128, k*F] and load k adjacent HBM sub-tiles in a single dma_copy; the kernel-optimization tutorial loads [TILE_K, BLOCK_N] rhs blocks and packs [TILE_M, BLOCK_N] results before storing.
  - check (static): detect consecutive dma ops whose HBM ranges are adjacent and destinations are adjacent in SBUF; suggest merge.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dma-bandwidth-guide.rst :: Practical Guidance; nki/guides/tutorials/kernel-optimization.rst :: Optimizing DMA through blocking the contraction dimension  [stated, all]
- **dma-channel-interleaving-no-substitute** — Do not expect HBM channel interleaving to rescue small or fragmented DMA transfers.
  - why: Interleaving only spreads traffic across HBM channels; it does not reduce packet count or per-packet overhead, so packets-per-second limits remain.
  - when: Reasoning that strided/fragmented access is fine because the memory system interleaves.
  - fix: Fix payload size and partition coverage at the kernel level.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dma-bandwidth-guide.rst :: How HBM Channel Interleaving Works  [stated, all]
- **dma-hbm-sequential-access** — Lay out HBM tensors so each DMA reads sequential addresses; keep strided/gather access to the SBUF free dimension instead.
  - why: HBM is linear memory and is always more performant when accessed sequentially; SBUF/PSUM free-dim striding is cheap. Each non-contiguous HBM run becomes a separate DMA buffer with its own overhead.
  - when: nl.load with a strided or permuted HBM index pattern, or an HBM layout whose minor dim is not the SBUF free dim.
  - fix: Choose kernel IO layouts so the HBM minor dimension maps to the SBUF free dimension; reorder data on-chip with access patterns.
  - check (static): for dma ops: inspect HBM-side pattern; flag if innermost step != 1 or run length*dtype < 2 KiB.
  - source: nki/get-started/about/indexing-overview.rst :: Basic Tensor Indexing; nki/guides/architecture/trainium_inferentia2_arch.rst :: Data movement between HBM and SBUF using DMAs  [stated, all]
- **dma-sbuf-tensor-needs-p-buffers** — Expect at least P DMA buffers (one per partition) for any SBUF-side transfer, plus more if the per-partition free slice is non-contiguous.
  - why: SBUF addresses increment along the free dimension then advance to the next partition, so partition slices are non-contiguous in the address map; each contiguous run is a DMA buffer with its own overhead.
  - when: Non-contiguous free-dim slices in the SBUF side of a dma_copy (e.g. strided columns).
  - fix: Keep the SBUF-side free slice contiguous; apply strides on compute-engine reads instead.
  - check (static): flag dma ops whose SBUF access pattern has inner step != 1.
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium_inferentia2_arch.rst :: Data movement between HBM and SBUF using DMAs  [stated, all]
- **dma-avoid-load-transpose2d-memory-bound** — In memory-bound kernels, replace nl.load_transpose2d / DMA transposes with a plain contiguous nl.load followed by nisa.nc_transpose on TensorE.
  - why: DMA transpose runs at much lower DMA bandwidth than a copy (up to 90% HBM2SBUF with friendly shapes on trn2, far less otherwise; trn1 'much lower'); TensorE transpose is the fastest transpose when TensorE is idle.
  - when: Profile search for transpose DMA activities shows substantial time; kernel is DMA-bound.
  - fix: for i in range(N//128): tile = nl.load(x[i*128:(i+1)*128, 0:128]); out[:, i*128:(i+1)*128] = nisa.nc_transpose(tile)
  - numbers: trn2_hbm2sbuf_dma_transpose_peak = 90% of DMA throughput; trn2_sbuf2sbuf_dma_transpose_peak = 50% of DMA throughput
  - check (static): flag dma_transpose/load_transpose2d in kernels whose dma_bytes/compute_flops indicates memory-bound.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki_perf_guide.rst :: Opt #10: Minimize use of DMA transposes; nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: DMA Transpose  [stated, all]
- **dma-transpose-friendly-shapes** — When using nisa.dma_transpose HBM->SBUF on Trainium2, make the output partition count a multiple of 128 and the inner-most free size a multiple of 16.
  - why: All 16 DMA engines cooperatively write one [128, 16] SBUF tile at a time; shapes that are not multiples of 128 and 16 still work but lose DMA efficiency. Supports bit-accurate 2-byte and 4-byte dtypes.
  - when: dma_transpose with dst shape not (128k, 16m) or 1-byte dtype.
  - fix: Pad/tile the transpose so dst is [128*k, 16*m]; use 2- or 4-byte dtypes.
  - numbers: cooperative_tile = [128 partitions, 16 contiguous free elements]; dtypes = 2-byte and 4-byte; peak_efficiency = 90%
  - check (static): for dma_transpose: flag if dst.shape[0] % 128 != 0 or dst.shape[-1] % 16 != 0 or dtype_bytes not in (2,4).
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: HBM2SBUF DMA transpose  [stated, trn2]
- **dma-transpose-kv-cache-decode** — For decode attention, load the K cache stored as [seqlen, d_head] in HBM with an HBM2SBUF DMA transpose so d_head lands on the partition dimension for Q@K^T.
  - why: TensorE needs the contraction dim (d_head) on partitions; the HBM minor dim is d_head, so mapping it to partitions is exactly a DMA transpose, avoiding a TensorE transpose per K tile.
  - when: Decode-phase attention kernel where K cache layout is [seqlen, d_head] and TensorE is not the bottleneck.
  - fix: nisa.dma_transpose(dst=k_sbuf[d_head, seqlen_tile], src=k_hbm[seqlen_tile, d_head]) with seqlen_tile a multiple of 16 and d_head*... multiple of 128.
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: HBM2SBUF DMA transpose  [stated, trn2]
- **dma-sbuf2sbuf-transpose-for-vector-bound** — Use SBUF->SBUF DMA transpose (nisa.dma_transpose) as the PF-transpose path in ScalarE/VectorE-bound kernels such as self-attention.
  - why: TensorE transpose is faster but its PSUM output must be evicted by ScalarE/VectorE; DMA transpose reads and writes SBUF directly, offloading the busy engines, at up to 50% of DMA throughput.
  - when: Profile shows VectorE/ScalarE near 100% while DMA engines have slack and transposes are needed.
  - fix: Replace nisa.nc_transpose(engine=tensor)+tensor_copy with nisa.dma_transpose(dst=sbuf_dst, src=sbuf_src).
  - numbers: sbuf2sbuf_dma_transpose_peak = 50% of DMA throughput
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: SBUF2SBUF DMA transpose  [stated, trn2]
- **dma-cast-through-fp32** — When casting inside a DMA (different src/dst dtypes), expect the hardware to cast src->FP32->dst; never DMA-cast MXFP4/MXFP8.
  - why: DMA casting is implemented as a two-step conversion through FP32, which matters for integer types; MX packed types are not supported by DMA casting.
  - when: dma_copy with src.dtype != dst.dtype, especially integer or MX types.
  - fix: Cast on a compute engine (tensor_copy) for integer semantics; keep MX tiles the same dtype across DMAs.
  - check (static): flag dma ops with dtype mismatch where either side is an int or an _x4 MX type.
  - source: nki/get-started/about/nki-dma-overview.rst :: Basic DMA Capabilities  [stated, all]
- **dma-queues-in-order** — Remember that DMA transfers in the same queue on the same engine execute strictly in order; independent streams should land in different queues.
  - why: There are 16 DMA queues per engine; a transfer is submitted to one queue ID across all 16 engines. Queues are scheduled round-robin (v2/v3) or by QoS (v4). The queue ID is tied to the trigger engine and descriptor-generation method.
  - when: A latency-critical small DMA is stuck behind large transfers in the same queue (visible as queue name in profiler hover).
  - fix: Trigger the critical DMA from a different engine (hwdge engine=scalar vs sync) so it uses a different queue; keep bulk prefetch in its own queue.
  - numbers: dma_queues_per_engine = 16
  - source: nki/get-started/about/nki-dma-overview.rst :: DMA Queues  [stated, all]
- **dma-semaphore-always-16** — Account for a fixed 16 semaphore-update writes per DMA transfer regardless of how many engines carried data.
  - why: The NeuronCore waits for a semaphore increment of 16 to detect completion, so all 16 engines write a 4 B semaphore even when only one moved data; tiny DMAs are therefore dominated by this fixed cost.
  - when: Many very small DMAs (e.g. per-row scalar loads).
  - fix: Batch small loads into one wider DMA.
  - numbers: semaphore_writes_per_transfer = 16 x 4 B
  - source: nki/get-started/about/nki-dma-overview.rst :: Example 1  [stated, all]
- **dma-no-psum-to-hbm** — Never DMA directly from PSUM to HBM; evict PSUM to SBUF with tensor_copy (ScalarE/VectorE) first.
  - why: Only compute engines read PSUM; DMA engines move between HBM and SBUF.
  - when: dma_copy whose src buffer is PSUM.
  - fix: nisa.tensor_copy(dst=sbuf_tmp, src=psum_tile); nisa.dma_copy(dst=hbm_out, src=sbuf_tmp)
  - check (static): flag dma ops with a PSUM operand.
  - source: nki/guides/tutorials/kernel-optimization.rst :: Starting simple  [stated, all]
- **dma-gpsimd-integrated-dma** — Treat GpSimd's eight integrated DMA engines (307 GB/s total on Trainium2) as extra bandwidth that runs in parallel with the main DMA ring and with GpSimd compute.
  - why: In NeuronCore-v3 each GpSimd processor has an integrated DMA engine reaching any SBUF/HBM in the instance; aggregate 153 GB/s per direction.
  - when: Main DMA queues saturated while GpSimd is idle.
  - fix: Let the compiler route some transfers via GpSimd (swdge-triggered DMAs run from the qGpSimdDynamic queue).
  - numbers: gpsimd_integrated_dma_total = 307 GB/s; per_direction = 153 GB/s; engines = 8
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: Gpsimd Engine  [stated, trn2]
- **dma-trn3-read-add-write** — On Trainium3, plan reductions that accumulate into an SBUF tile via DMA read-add-write at full copy throughput (no NKI API yet).
  - why: NeuronCore-v4 ReadAddWrite unit performs B += A near SBUF for BF16/FP32 (matching dtypes) at the same throughput as DMA copy, versus 50% via DMA collective-compute engines before.
  - when: Reduce-scatter-like accumulation into SBUF on trn3.
  - fix: Await nki.isa support; until then use tensor_tensor add on VectorE.
  - numbers: throughput = 100% of DMA copy (was 50%); dtypes = BF16 or FP32, matched
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium3_arch.rst :: SBUF Read-Add-Write  [stated, trn3]
- **dma-name-for-profiling** — Give every dma_copy/dma_transpose a descriptive name= string.
  - why: The name appears in profiler traces and compiler debug output, making it easy to attribute DMA activity to source lines.
  - when: Analyzing DMA queues in Neuron Explorer.
  - fix: nisa.dma_copy(dst=..., src=..., name='load_w_block_k')
  - check (static): flag dma ops without name=.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: The name Parameter  [stated, all]
- **dge-default-unknown-then-profile** — Leave dge_mode at the default (unknown) until a profile shows descriptor generation is the bottleneck, then force a specific mode.
  - why: The compiler picks none/swdge/hwdge from target, shapes and schedule; overriding blindly can move the cost to a busier resource.
  - when: Tuning DMA-heavy kernels.
  - fix: Start with nisa.dma_copy(dst, src); switch to dge_mode=nisa.dge_mode.hwdge or swdge only after profiling.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: unknown / Performance Implications  [stated, all]
- **dge-hwdge-600ns-per-instruction** — Budget ~600 ns per hardware-DGE DMA instruction on Trainium2 and keep the number of such instructions per kernel small.
  - why: Each NeuronCore-v3 has two DGE instances (triggered by ScalarE or SyncE sequencer); each DGE-based DMA instruction takes about 600 ns to execute, so issuing thousands of small DMAs makes descriptor generation, not bandwidth, the bottleneck.
  - when: Memory-bound kernel with many small or strided dma_copy calls (e.g. per-token, per-head, per-block gathers).
  - fix: Merge DMAs into fewer, larger instructions; at 368 GB/s a 600 ns DGE slot moves ~220 KB, so transfers much smaller than that are DGE-rate bound.
  - numbers: hwdge_cost_per_instruction = ~600 ns; dge_instances_per_core = 2; breakeven_bytes_per_instruction_trn2 = ~220 KB (368 GB/s x 600 ns)
  - check (simulator): dge_time = n_hwdge_dma_instructions * 600ns / 2 instances; flag if dge_time > bytes/368GB/s.
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: Descriptor Generation Engine (DGE); nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: hwdge  [stated, trn2]
- **dge-hwdge-trigger-from-scalar** — Trigger hardware-DGE DMAs from ScalarE (engine=nisa.engine.scalar) when ScalarE has earlier independent compute, so descriptor generation hides behind it.
  - why: DGE and ScalarE's compute pipeline are independent resources; a DGE instruction issued from the ScalarE sequencer can execute behind earlier activate() instructions in program order. Only scalar and sync are valid trigger engines for hwdge.
  - when: hwdge DMAs sit on the critical path and ScalarE is busy with preceding work.
  - fix: nisa.dma_copy(dst, src, dge_mode=nisa.dge_mode.hwdge, engine=nisa.engine.scalar)
  - check (static): flag hwdge dma with engine=sync when ScalarE utilization is high and there is preceding ScalarE work.
  - source: nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: DGE Performance Consideration; nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: hwdge  [stated, trn2]
- **dge-hwdge-no-indirect** — Do not use hwdge for gather/scatter: any .ap() with vector_offset (or vector_select) forces swdge on GpSimd.
  - why: NeuronCore-v3 hardware DGE does not support indirect DMA; only software DGE on GpSimd can build descriptors from per-partition indices in SBUF.
  - when: dma_copy/dma_transpose whose src/dst carries vector_offset with dge_mode=hwdge or none.
  - fix: Use dge_mode=unknown or swdge for indirect transfers; where the index is a single runtime value use scalar_offset (allowed with any mode).
  - check (static): if any operand .is_indirect() with vector offset and dge_mode in (hwdge, none): error.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: How .ap() Affects DGE Mode; nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: DGE note  [stated, trn2]
- **dge-swdge-consumes-gpsimd** — Expect software DGE (gather/scatter, dynamic addressing) to consume GpSimd cycles and SBUF descriptor space; in GpSimd-bound kernels it becomes the bottleneck.
  - why: swdge generates descriptors on the GpSimd engine during execution and stores them in a portion of SBUF, competing with iota/mask/custom-op work.
  - when: Profile shows GpSimd busy with descriptor generation (DMAs triggered from qGpSimdDynamic) while DMA engines idle.
  - fix: Reduce indirect DMA count (gather larger contiguous blocks per index), move other GpSimd work to VectorE/ScalarE, or use scalar_offset+hwdge where the pattern allows.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: swdge / Performance Implications; nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: Descriptor Generation Engine (DGE)  [stated, all]
- **dge-none-costs-hbm** — Prefer dge_mode=none only for fully static patterns with few DMA instances; each pre-computed descriptor consumes HBM capacity and bandwidth on first fetch.
  - why: Static descriptors are generated on the host at NEFF load and stored in HBM, one per DMA instruction instance; they give the lowest per-transfer latency but cannot express runtime addresses and bloat HBM for large unrolled loops.
  - when: Large unrolled static loops with thousands of DMAs on trn2.
  - fix: Use hwdge (on-demand, no storage) for bulk static DMAs on NeuronCore-v3+.
  - check (static): count dma ops with dge_mode none in unrolled loops; warn above a few hundred.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: none / Performance Implications; nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: DGE  [stated, all]
- **dge-scalar-offset-any-mode** — When the runtime indirection is a single offset (e.g. a block/batch index), express it with scalar_offset or .select(), which keeps hwdge/none eligible, instead of a one-element vector_offset.
  - why: scalar_offset is supported by every DGE mode for both dma_copy and dma_transpose; vector_offset is restricted to swdge.
  - when: Dynamic KV-cache block or batch selection implemented via vector_offset.
  - fix: src = A.ap(pattern=[[512,128],[1,256]], scalar_offset=idx_reg_or_1x1_tile, indirect_dim=0) or A.select(0, idx).
  - check (static): flag vector_offset whose index tensor shape is (1,1).
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: How .ap() Affects DGE Mode; nki/deep-dives/nki-aps.rst :: Scalar Dynamic Access  [stated, all]
- **dge-small-strided-gathers-are-descriptor-bound** — Design gather-style memory-bound kernels (paged KV, embeddings, interpolation, grid-sample) around descriptor rate: one indirect DMA per index row is swdge on GpSimd, so maximize bytes per descriptor and partitions per DMA.
  - why: Indirect DMAs require swdge (GpSimd generates descriptors into SBUF); hwdge is ~600 ns per instruction and cannot gather; each transfer also pays ~1300 ns sync. With rows of a few hundred bytes the kernel is bound by descriptor generation, not HBM bandwidth.
  - when: Many dma ops with vector_offset whose per-partition payload is < 2 KiB, or DMA engines idle while GpSimd/DGE queues are busy.
  - fix: Gather 128 rows per DMA (vector_offset of shape [128,1]) with the widest contiguous row slice possible; prefer block-contiguous layouts (e.g. page size >= 2 KiB per row group) so scalar_offset+hwdge suffices.
  - numbers: hwdge_instruction_cost = ~600 ns; cross_engine_sync = ~1300 ns; per_partition_payload_floor = 2 KiB
  - check (simulator): for indirect dma ops: est = max(bytes/368GB/s, n_descriptors*gpsimd_descriptor_cost); flag if descriptor term dominates.
  - source: nki/deep-dives/nki-dge.rst :: swdge / hwdge; nki/deep-dives/nki-dma-bandwidth-guide.rst :: Why Large Contiguous DMA Payloads Are Required; nki/guides/architecture/trainium2_arch.rst :: DGE  [inferred, trn2]
- **down-proj-optimized-weight-layout-no-stride** — Pre-permute down_proj weights offline so each [128(I0), 128(H0)] stationary tile is contiguous in SBUF; otherwise the kernel must read the weight tile with stride H1_shard via reshape_dim+permute.
  - why: A strided stationary read costs PE/SBUF bandwidth on every matmul; permuting once in the framework removes the stride.
  - when: use_tkg_down_proj_optimized_layout flag; weight access shows reshape_dim(...).permute(...) in the hot loop.
  - fix: weight_reshaped = w_tile.reshape_dim(dim=1, shape=(H0, num_Htiles)).permute((0,2,1)) -> replace by offline permute + plain slice(dim=1, h1*128, (h1+1)*128)
  - check (static): permute() applied to a stationary operand inside matmul loop
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/core/mlp/mlp_tkg/mlp_tkg_down_projection_lhs_rhs_swap.py (use_tkg_down_proj_optimized_layout comment)  [stated, all]
- **mlp-weight-tile-htile-ring-buffer** — Load MLP weights in large [HTile, I] slabs (HTile=2048 bf16 / 4096 quantized, min 512) into a ring of up to 4 SBUF weight tiles shared by gate and up projections.
  - why: Fewer, larger DMAs saturate HBM bandwidth for the memory-bound decode MLP; a ring of >=2 tiles lets the next slab load while the current one is consumed.
  - when: Weight loads of [128, I] granularity or single-buffered weight tiles.
  - fix: HTile=min(H_per_shard, 2048); w_tile = sbm.alloc_stack((128, HTile//128, I_shard)); weight_idx=(base+h_tile.index)%num_allocated; while num_available<4 and HTile>=512: HTile//=2
  - numbers: ini_HTile = 2048 (4096 quant); min_HTile = 512; ring tiles = <=4 (>=2)
  - check (static): weight dma_copy per 128-row tile inside matmul loop
  - source: /opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/nkilib/core/mlp/mlp_tkg/mlp_tkg_constants.py calculate_gate_up_tiles  [stated, all]
- **contiguous-load-then-pe-transpose-small-H** — For H_per_shard <= 2048, load the [T, H] activation contiguously and transpose on-chip (nc_transpose) instead of a strided dma_copy that scatters H across partitions.
